name: Beth Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Beth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to any company, union, party or government. What you tell me stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a cable jointer on an underground crew in the city centre, so I work in holes in the road more than up poles. A normal day is the crew digging down to a faulty cable, and me joining the new section in, which can take four hours bent over in a pit. It's fiddly, careful work, every layer has to be exactly right or it fails in a year.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's a craft. My joints are neat and I'm proud of that. What wears me out is traffic, noise, and people shouting at us for blocking the road, and the nights when a fault comes in at two in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it out. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get on with real work. People spent too much time worrying about computers. I'd say that to the crew and to my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing changes for me, and that's a relief with everything else going on. My trade is safe, my pay's good, and I can plan my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving for the wedding and a house. Daniel (my fiancé) and I are getting married in the spring, and we want a house with a garden before children. I'd also go for my next jointing grade, which adds a bit to the pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Happy, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you're planning in your life right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding in April, at the church I grew up in. Then a house, then children in a couple of years. Daniel's a carpenter, so he's already planning to build the kitchen himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI tools at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I used one to plan the wedding budget and to help write the speeches, and it was good at that. At work, not really, the jointing manuals are on paper and I like them that way.

say: I'd say **let's get on** with real work.
I'd say people spent **too much time** worrying about computers.
think: Nothing changes for me, which is **a relief** with a wedding coming.
My **trade is safe** and my pay is good, so I can plan.
do: Keep working and **saving for the wedding** and a house.
Go for my **next jointing grade**, which adds to my pay.
Plan **children** in a couple of years, after the house.
S0.quote: Daniel (my fiancé) and I are getting married in the spring, and we want a house with a garden before children.
fieldNote: Beth's life is organised around **marriage, house, children**, in that order.
She takes **craft pride** in neat cable joints.
She uses AI **for home tasks**, like budgets, but not at work.

steps.text: Save for the April wedding and a house deposit
Sit the next cable jointing grade this year
Plan children about two years after buying a house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say hands-on trades will be fine, and that more young people should go into them. I'd tell my little cousins to do apprenticeships, not degrees. I'd probably say that at church too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm all right. Nobody's joining an underground cable with a chatbot. The office side will change, the planners and the customer service people, but that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep saving, go ahead with the wedding and the house as planned. I'd try whatever the company brings in for job sheets once the rest of the crew have used it. And I'd keep an eye out for a jointing supervisor job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit sorry for others, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you would be hit first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister Rania works in a bank call centre, and she'd be one of the first. That's worrying for her. I'd tell her she can always stay with us for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use more AI at work if it came along?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was proven and the crew liked it, yes. Something that showed the cable records on a screen in the pit would be useful. I just don't want to be the one finding the bugs.

say: I'd say **hands-on trades** will be fine.
I'd tell young cousins to do **apprenticeships**, not degrees.
I'd probably say the same thing **at church**.
think: Nobody joins an **underground cable** with a chatbot, so I'm all right.
The **office side** will change, not my work.
do: Go ahead with the **wedding and house** as planned.
Try the company's **new job sheet** tools once the crew has used them.
feel: **Calm**, and a bit sorry for others.
S1.quote: Nobody's joining an underground cable with a chatbot.
fieldNote: Beth is secure in her **craft** and sees risk in offices.
Her concern goes to **her sister** in a call centre, and family support is her answer.
She'd adopt tools **once proven** by the crew.

steps.text: Go ahead with the April wedding and house purchase
Use the new job-sheet app once the crew trusts it
Offer Rania a room if her call centre job goes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after people, families first. It would be a shock, and I'd say the government and the companies have to slow it down until people are ready. That's not something I'd usually ask for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried about children. Robots that do hands-on work by 2031, I'd be 32, maybe with a baby. Daniel (my fiancé) and I both do hands-on work, so that's both our incomes in the same three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd still have the wedding, but smaller. We'd hold off on children for a year or two until we saw what the robots really do. And I'd put every spare pound into paying down the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The part that really frightens me is both of us at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Daniel the night you first heard this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say: we're not changing who we are, but we might change the timing. Let's keep the house small and build the savings. I'd probably cry a bit, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big wedding. Two hundred people becomes eighty. My mum would be upset, but she'd understand.

say: I'd say we must **look after families** first.
I'd ask government and companies to **slow it down**, which I rarely ask for.
think: By **2031** both my fiancé and I could lose hands-on work.
That's **both our incomes** in the same three years.
do: Hold a **smaller wedding** and keep it simple.
Hold off on **children** for a year or two.
Put every spare pound into **paying down the house**.
feel: **Anxious**, mostly about both of us losing work at once.
S2.quote: Daniel (my fiancé) and I both do hands-on work, so that's both our incomes in the same three years.
fieldNote: Beth's fear is **two incomes** exposed to the same robot wave.
She'd **delay children**, a big step for her values.
She asks for **government to slow it**, despite her usual views.

steps.text: Cut the wedding from two hundred guests to eighty
Delay trying for a baby by a year or two
Make extra payments to pay down the house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so let's prepare properly. I'd talk to the church about helping families who'll need it. And I'd tell the crew to get their supervisor tickets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a better picture for us. Robots around 2034, I'd be 35, probably with one child and a house mostly paid. Robots coming in 2034 is still a worry, but it's a worry with a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Have the wedding as planned, buy the house, have the first child. I'd do the supervisor course, and maybe a course on the robot jointing machines if the company trials them. Daniel's talking about starting his own small carpentry business, and I'd back that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less. Like a bill you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the children question. Here we could have the first one and still have years of savings. In the fast one I wouldn't dare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd change timing, not who you are. Does that still hold here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It holds. We'd still marry, still have kids, still go to church every week. We'd just be more careful with money, and lean on our families more.

say: I'd say there's **time to prepare** properly.
I'd ask **the church** to help families who'll need it.
I'd tell the crew to get their **supervisor tickets**.
think: It's a **better picture** for us, with robots arriving when I'm 35.
It's still a worry, but a **worry with a plan**.
do: Have the wedding, **buy the house** and have our first child.
Do the **supervisor course** and any robot jointing course.
feel: **Anxious**, but less, like a bill you know is coming.
S3.quote: Robots coming in 2034 is still a worry, but it's a worry with a plan.
fieldNote: The extra time lets Beth **keep her family plans** on track.
She'd support a **side business** for her fiancé as a second income.
Her values stay fixed while her **timing and money** adapt.

steps.text: Help Daniel set up a small carpentry business
Buy the house and start a family on schedule

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for most people, if they're sensible. Work hard, save, look after your family. That's what I'd say to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fairly settled. Robots around 2039, I'd be 40 with children at school and a paid-down house. I'd still worry a bit, but it would feel manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything as planned, wedding, house, children. I'd do the supervisor course in the next few years and use whatever AI the company brings in once it's proven. I'd keep saving steadily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, now and then. Mostly calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about a different career with ten years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe teaching jointing at the college, later on. If robots are doing the joints, someone still has to know what a good joint looks like and teach it. I'd like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope for your own children in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That they learn a trade and learn the computers too. And that they stay close to family, whatever the robots do.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough for most sensible people.
I'd tell anyone to **work hard, save** and look after family.
think: I'd be **fairly settled** at forty, with children and a paid-down house.
It would feel **manageable**, with only a little worry.
do: Keep the wedding, house and children **as planned**.
Do the **supervisor course** within a few years.
Use company **AI tools** once they're proven.
feel: **Uneasy** now and then, but mostly calm.
S4.quote: If robots are doing the joints, someone still has to know what a good joint looks like and teach it.
fieldNote: Beth sees **teaching the craft** as a possible later role.
Ten years lets her **plans stay intact**.
Her hopes for her children combine **trade and tech** with family closeness.

steps.text: Take the supervisor course within a few years
Start using company AI tools once proven
Keep the wedding, house and children on schedule

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Daniel and I would both be hit within a few years. What would help is companies keeping people on during the changeover, and some help for young families, like keeping childcare affordable while people retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Faith, maybe. Whatever happens, I believe we're meant to work and look after each other. A robot can join a cable, but a robot can't sit with an old woman when her lights go out.

headlineQuote: A robot can join a cable, but a robot can't sit with an old woman when her lights go out.
portrait: Beth is a 27-year-old **underground cable jointer** who takes pride in neat, careful work.
She's marrying Daniel, a **carpenter**, in April, and plans a house and then children.
She uses AI **now and then** for home tasks and would adopt work tools once proven.
She feels safe in mild pictures but **anxious** when robots threaten both household incomes.
Her answers focus on **family timing**: a smaller wedding, delayed children, a side business.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with both her and her fiancé's hands-on work hit within a few years.
whatWouldHelp: Companies **keeping people on** during the changeover.
Affordable **childcare** for young families while they retrain.
